summary:
SPHEREx WATCH is a browser-based investigation platform that helps people explore NASA SPHEREx infrared observations and examine how the sky changes across repeated visits.

We developed an interactive Sky Monitor, a local right ascension and declination search, a FITS observation archive, temporal image viewing, and a candidate-review workspace.

A Python pipeline uses Astropy, NumPy, and Pillow to read FITS files, extract metadata, and generate image previews for the web. When observations are sufficiently compatible, the workflow can support alignment and difference-image analysis; otherwise, the interface avoids reporting unsupported motion measurements.
Users can inspect observations, record investigation notes, and export reports.
By making complex multi-epoch astronomical data easier to explore and review, SPHEREx WATCH supports transparent, evidence-based investigations. It is a research prototype, not a claim of a new celestial discovery.
details:
SPHEREx WATCH — Project Details

The Problem

NASA's SPHEREx mission observes the sky across 102 infrared spectral channels. Repeated observations create opportunities to study changing and potentially moving sources. However, astronomical FITS files contain complex image data and metadata that are difficult for non-specialists to explore.

SPHEREx WATCH addresses this challenge by transforming astronomical observations into an interactive, accessible investigation platform.

Our Solution

We developed a web-based scientific exploration platform with six main components.

Sky Monitor: An interactive observation viewer where users can explore available sky images, inspect observation metadata, and search the local dataset using right ascension (RA) and declination (Dec).

Temporal Analysis: A workspace for comparing observations from different times. Users can select observation frames and use blink visualization to inspect changes. Difference-image processing is supported when the input observations satisfy the necessary compatibility and alignment conditions.

Candidate Investigation: A review workspace where users can inspect potential sources of interest, record investigation notes, and export structured reports. Candidate labels are preliminary and do not represent confirmed discoveries.

FITS Explorer: An archive interface for browsing processed NASA SPHEREx Level 2 observations, image previews, and metadata.

Data & Methodology: An educational section explaining SPHEREx, the processing workflow, scientific uncertainty, and the limitations of interpreting astronomical observations.

Landing Page: A visual introduction to the platform, its purpose, and the investigation workflow.

How It Works

The platform uses NASA SPHEREx FITS observations obtained through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

Python scripts process the FITS files, extract image data and metadata, and generate PNG previews and JSON catalogs. The frontend loads these resources to provide interactive visualization and investigation tools.

The processing workflow considers observation time, wavelength, image quality, and celestial coordinate information. Reliable temporal comparison requires compatible observations and appropriate image registration.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy, Astropy, Pillow
  • Astronomical formats: FITS, WCS metadata
  • Data exchange: JSON
  • Interface design: Figma
  • Development and distribution: Git, GitHub, Windows PowerShell

Innovation and Impact

SPHEREx WATCH combines astronomical data exploration, temporal visualization, and candidate review in one accessible interface.

Its main contribution is not claiming to discover a new planet or object, but making scientific evidence easier to inspect, compare, and communicate.

The platform is intended for students, astronomy enthusiasts, hackathon participants, and researchers interested in exploring infrared observations.

Scientific Integrity and Limitations

The project distinguishes real NASA observations from demonstration data.

A change in image appearance does not automatically indicate physical motion. Different wavelengths, image quality, registration errors, and observational conditions may produce apparent differences.

The current prototype does not establish a new planet's identity, distance, or orbit. Additional observations, uncertainty analysis, and independent verification would be necessary for such conclusions.

SPHEREx WATCH demonstrates how open space-science data can support transparent, collaborative, and evidence-based exploration.
